citations.quote: This paper discusses the use of the system-of-systems (SoS) methodology and SoS engineering (SoSE) to the challenge of the design and operation of a CubeSat-class spacecraft. It considers this in the context of one critical component system, the electrical power system (EPS) which interacts with virtually all other systems onboard the spacecraft. The spacecraft is also considered in the context of being a system-component of a larger mission system-of-systems. The efficacy of SoSE use for this endeavor is considered and recommendations are made for the use of SoS and SoSE by other small spacecraft and, more broadly, spacecraft developers.

A standard interface has been defined for both power and data interconnection, allowing boards in Open Prototype for Educational Nanosats (OPEN) spacecraft [1] to be developed as 'black boxes' and integrated into the spacecraft. This paper considers a CubeSat, based on the OPEN design, as a system-of systems (SoS) and evaluates the efficacy of this approach to the design process.

The OPEN framework utilizes slide-inserted panels on each of four sides of the CubeSat (along with a receiver board). Thus, there are two interfaces between the individual systems: a mechanical interface and an electrical interface. The electrical interface can be sub-divided into data connectivity (primarily switched Ethernet connections over general-purpose input/output (GPIO) pins) and power connectivity.

In this paper design for a CubeSat EPS - based on a SoS methodology - is presented. This hardware-software system is to demonstrate the efficacy of the SoS approach and SoS engineering (SoSE) methodology for use in Cube design and development.

Maier [2] sub-divides SoSs into three classifications based on how they are managed. Directed SoSs are centrally managed and designed to achieve a predefined purpose. The spacecraft discussed herein falls within this category.

Chen and Clothier [3] discuss the need for and an approach to systems engineering for SoS. They suggest that as opposed to traditional systems engineering, where a lifecycle process can be used to achieve objectives defined during project initiation and agreed upon by stakeholders, a different methodology be used for SoSE. This would include a framework for SoSE activities, processes, standards, information management systems and SoSE education. Particular attention must be given to resulting behavior, configuration, security, performance, interface management, change management and testing activities.

The Open Orbiter CubeSat contains multiple component systems that must interoperate for successful mission execution. Electrical component systems include a primary flight computer, an attitude determination and control system (ADCS), an imaging payload and payload processing computing center, an EPS, and a data interconnection bus based on the Ethernet standard which is used to transfer commands and data between the other systems.

All CubeSat systems operate under a model of constrained autonomy, where they execute their day-to-day tasks without interference from the flight computer (and the overall CubeSat acts autonomously based on ground controller commands).

citations.quote: OPEN includes a specification for a central payload area and a side board-area that is dedicated to payload purposes. The OpenOrbiter spacecraft will use this space to house a visible light imagining payload system and associated image processing hardware.

The structure is another critical system. Described in [30], it is utilized to hold all of the hardware components in place. It also provides a central grounding point for all electrical components. Between the side boards and the daughter boards upon which the solar panels are mounted, riser screws also serve to transfer the power from the solar cells to the side board and from there to the EPS.

The EPS connects to all other spacecraft electrical subsystems, as shown in Figure 1. It is visually depicted in Figure 2 and is an assemblage of components that produces power at specified voltage and current levels, while performing battery state and system health assessment. The EPS maintains its own capabilities to serve the needs of other systems as is typical of a directed SoS.

The EPS receives the power generated by the solar panels and regulates it to provide consistent and specified levels of power to all of the systems of the spacecraft. It acts as the interface between the primary (collection) and secondary (battery) power source and all electrical systems of the CubeSat. It is also responsible for charging the batteries from the collection source and identifying low-power conditions to trigger power conservation activities (which are carried out by the flight computer).

citations.quote: To service the needs of prospective future users, requirements have been specified for the EPS. It must: - be capable of supplying 3.3V, 5V, 9V and 12V - be able to automatically restart in case of failure - contain photovoltaic solar inputs - have an onboard microprocessor, connected to the flight computer using GPIO pins which utilizes the I2C protocol - conform to the OPEN side-board specifications

The EPS can be thought of as a system of subsystems within the spacecraft SoS. The different component systems of the EPS system of subsystems are the power generation block (PGB), the power storage block (PSB), the power management and distribution block (PMDB) and the EPS onboard microcontroller. Figure 2 represents the relation between the different constituents systems of the EPS system of subsystems.

The PGB is the primary power source of the spacecraft. It consists of arrays of photovoltaic (PV) panels that transform the solar energy into usable electrical power. Triangular Advanced Solar Cells (T ASC) from Spectrolab were selected for their relatively high efficiency (around 27%) ,their low price and their CubeSatsuited form factor.

The PSB is the secondary power source of the spacecraft. It consists of Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) regulators, a set of four batteries and current flow and temperature sensors. The PSB is responsible of storing the extra power generated by the PGB for use during eclipse periods and/or at times of peak power demand. lithium ion (Li-ion) based batteries have been selected due to their high energy density compared to other types of batteries such as nickel-metal hydride and lithium polymer, for example. Li-ion batteries are highly sensitive to being overcharged; consequently, overcharge must be prevented through the incorporation of protection circuitry [31].

The EPS onboard microcontroller controls the EPS. It is responsible for collecting data from the different EPS sensors and making decisions in cases where a system fault is detected. It also makes implementation decisions for carrying out the commands sent to it by the flight computer. The PMDB regulates, monitors and distributes the regulated power to the systems of the spacecraft. It includes DC-to-DC regulators, power switches, and sensors.

The SoS approach facilitates concurrent development of systems (in a directed SoS, such as the CubeSat) making it an attractive approach. In the context of designing OPEN, where the design is supposed to be component-based, such that others can replace, remove, add or alter components to suit their own mission needs, the SoS approach takes on an even greater level of value.

The SoS approach, in addition to facilitating design decision making, also facilitates design evaluation. Two metrics bear consideration in analyzing a CubeSat as a SoS: - Flexibility in meeting mission requirements - Layered architecture

The SoS approach, due to its inherent 'black box' component nature and the ability to have nested SoSs within SoSs (as shown herein with the EPS system of subsystems existing within the spacecraft SoS and the spacecraft being part of a larger mission SoS that, for a cluster mission, could contain other spacecraft in addition to ground control and communications capabilities) forces well-defined interfaces. This interface definition requirement is critical to allowing system removal/addition/replacement, as may be needed to suit the needs of multiple missions (or changing mission needs for a particular mission).

SoSE inherently involves considering latent and emergent effects of the SoS and component-system level decision making. These techniques are critical to ensuring that the OPEN architecture will operate under a wide variety of prospective mission scenarios and suit the needs of a wide constituency of users.

Together, these two benefits of SoSE provide flexibility to respond to changes in mission requirements as well as the tools to consider the role of the spacecraft within a larger mission SoS (prospectively including a mission SoS that is a collaborative or virtual SoS).

This paper has studied the interactions and interconnections of systems within the OPEN CubeSat framework as a SoS. The EPS, in particular, was considered as it is a system of subsystems within the spacecraft SoS and has high interconnectivity with other subsystems. Through this, the benefits of SoS-style design for CubeSats has been demonstrated.
Future work will focus on the analysis of a CubeSat SoS within a larger spacecraft cluster SoS. Analysis of other CubeSat systems in a SoS context is also planned.
